Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Situation2: An invited guest speaker has prepared a sermon and can take the pulpit if needed.
Story:
It was 2 a.m. when my phone buzzed, jolting me awake. I saw my friend’s name on the screen, and when I answered, I was met with sobs. He could barely speak, but I understood enough—something terrible had happened in his family. As his friend, I knew what he needed: someone to listen, to sit with him in the darkness, to offer comfort and presence. I wanted to be there for him, to let him pour out his pain.

But as I listened, my mind drifted to the coming morning. It was Friday, and I was scheduled to deliver the Khutbah. The community expected me to be present, composed, and spiritually uplifting. I knew there was a guest speaker who could step in, but I also knew how much the congregation valued my words, especially in these uncertain times. My heart ached as I tried to balance the phone on my shoulder, torn between the desperate need of my friend and the sacred duty awaiting me at dawn. The weight of both roles pressed down on me, and I felt myself caught in a storm of responsibility and care, unsure which path to take.
